bibliography.abstract: Understanding how transportation research capacity is built and sustained requires empirical evidence on who enters the academic workforce, where they are trained, and how the workforce’s composition evolves over time. This paper provides a field-level measurement baseline for the U.S. transportation research workforce using a harmonized roster of 553 transportation-focused faculty across 151 ranked U.S. civil and environmental engineering departments assembled from publicly available sources. Positioned at the intersection of science, geography of knowledge, and academic labor market research, the study characterizes the geographic origins of the workforce by tracing where faculty completed their undergraduate education, a pre-doctoral indicator of how the field sources advanced human capital from global higher education systems. Two patterns emerge. First, faculty with undergraduate training in the United States represent the largest single source of workforce capacity (approximately one third) but do not constitute a majority. China is the second largest origin (just over one fifth), followed by a broad set of countries spanning many world regions. Second, the origins of newly entering faculty have shifted across cohorts defined by Ph.D. completion year: the domestic share has declined since the 1990s while the share trained in China has increased. These results indicate that the U.S. transportation academic workforce draws on global higher education and mobility systems. They provide an empirical baseline for transportation programs, professional societies, and federal agencies concerned with research capacity, knowledge diffusion, and workforce resilience.
bibliography.title: Global sources of the U.S. transportation research workforce

en.caveats: The study's scope is limited to faculty within civil and environmental engineering departments, which may exclude transportation researchers working in other academic disciplines like urban planning, geography, or economics.
en.what: This study analyzes a newly assembled roster of 553 transportation-focused faculty members across 151 ranked civil and environmental engineering departments in the United States to trace their undergraduate origins. The analysis reveals that while domestic-trained graduates represent the largest single group at approximately one-third of the workforce, they are not a majority, with China serving as the second-largest source at just over one-fifth. Longitudinal cohort analysis shows a declining share of U.S.-trained faculty and an increasing share of Chinese-trained faculty since the 1990s.
en.why: It establishes the first empirical, field-level baseline of the geographic origins of the U.S. transportation academic workforce, demonstrating that the country's research capacity is fundamentally dependent on global higher education and international talent mobility.
